vyr · measurement ledger · schema 3

The data

Every value recorded in history.jsonl, as flat sortable tables: the performance matrix cell by cell, every other recorded value one value per row, and one row per line of the file. Nothing is summarised, ranked or coloured here. Regenerated from the file by ./dev.py track (scripts/ledger.py) and never hand-edited; to change a number, take a measurement.

47 lines in the ledger · 47 runs · 656 matrix cells (546 measured) · 1921 other recorded values · latest 889543f fix(size,bench): finish #44 — fold out of the timed window on BOTH harnesses · how each number is produced: docs/performance.md.

Every numeric series, indexed to its own first observation

The tables carry levels; this carries change. The series share no unit — instructions per frame are tens of millions, heap is hundreds of thousands of bytes, ns per frame is hundreds, fold share is a fraction — so raw values on one axis would be meaningless, and a second y-axis would invent a correlation the data does not contain. Instead every series is divided by its own first recorded value and multiplied by 100. The axis is therefore dimensionless: 100 is that series’ own first observation, not a share of anything, and 50 means “half what it first was” for every line alike.

197 series on 46 runs. A series needs two observations to be a trend, so the 33 recorded only once are not drawn here — the tables have them. A further 4 cannot be indexed at all, because a first observation of 0 has no ratio to it (qemu-m4 · exact · 2 · fastpath_coverage_pct, qemu-m4 · exact · 3 · fastpath_coverage_pct, qemu-m4 · exact · s · fastpath_coverage_pct, qemu-m4 · exact · z · fastpath_coverage_pct) — also in the tables.

drag on the plot to zoom · double-click to reset

Hover a line to name it: the nearest series lifts, the rest fade, and the readout gives its key, the value the ledger recorded at that run, and its index. A gap is a gap — where a series has no observation at a run the line breaks rather than interpolating, and an observation with no neighbour is drawn as a single point. Series that never moved sit exactly on the 100 rule; they are drawn faintly because stability is evidence but it should not drown the lines that moved. Every value plotted here is also a row in the tables below.

Each row is one plotted series; the box shows it on the chart. Rows are ordered by swing — how far the indexed value travels from 100 — so the outliers that flatten everything else sit at the top. Hiding them rescales the y-axis to what is left. This changes only the chart; the tables below always hold every value.

Matrix cells

One row per measurement cell — platform × tier × opt-level × run — with every field the ledger carries for it, including the provenance of each figure and the written reason behind every null.

Click a column header to sort it; click again to reverse. Numeric columns sort numerically. Drag a header to reorder, and use its ⋮ menu to hide columns. A dotted-underlined value carries the reason the ledger recorded for it — hover to read it.

Every other recorded value

The host resolution ladder, anim and cross-ISA runs, bench medians, static size, stock-QEMU M4 quantities, real silicon, the projections the ledger derives and the matrix's own metadata. These sections have different shapes, so each recorded value is its own row: filter section or sort path to get a series back.

Click a column header to sort it; click again to reverse. Numeric columns sort numerically. Drag a header to reorder, and use its ⋮ menu to hide columns. A dotted-underlined value carries the reason the ledger recorded for it — hover to read it.

Runs

One row per line of history.jsonl, including the schema note and any commit that could not be measured. has … is 1 where the run recorded that section — rows are sparse because a run records what it measured and nothing else.

Click a column header to sort it; click again to reverse. Numeric columns sort numerically. Drag a header to reorder, and use its ⋮ menu to hide columns. A dotted-underlined value carries the reason the ledger recorded for it — hover to read it.
